title: Overview
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard is a self-service portal for Oracle Kubernetes Engine (OKE). Engineers create and operate clusters through approved workflows. Platform administrators define templates, identity roles, resource limits and protected operations. Terraform and OCI APIs execute the infrastructure work inside the customer environment.

title: Overview
heading: What is available
text: The current product focuses on OKE cluster provisioning and lifecycle operations: create, access, scale, upgrade and destroy. It includes templates, role-based visibility, resource limits, protected destroy requests, limit-increase requests, execution logs, Activity notifications and cost estimates. Infrayard provisions infrastructure for Kubernetes workloads. Application delivery, workload configuration and application-level operations stay within your existing processes. See product scope for the boundaries.

title: Overview
heading: How to get started
text: Request a demo to see a real workflow and discuss your OCI environment. Review your network, identity, permissions and deployment prerequisites. Start a monthly production subscription, choose an annual term or arrange an optional guided evaluation. Detailed release-specific deployment runbooks, customer Helm values and registry access are supplied during evaluation or onboarding. Public documentation describes the prerequisites and supported behaviour so you can assess fit first.

title: Overview
heading: Current capabilities and future plans
text: The releases and roadmap page separates available capabilities from planned work. Choose the product based on the functionality available in your contracted release.

title: Architecture
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard is installed in a customer-managed Kubernetes environment. It has no required Solvia-hosted SaaS control plane. The customer operates the installation and retains control of its OCI credentials, infrastructure state and operational records.

title: Architecture
heading: Components
text: Component Responsibility Web portal Cluster requests, lifecycle actions, access downloads and administration FastAPI service Authentication validation, resource validation, configuration, requests and lifecycle coordination PostgreSQL Cluster and job records, users, configuration, templates, requests and audit history Terraform runner Isolated execution for provisioning, scale, upgrade and destroy jobs OCI Object Storage Terraform state for Infrayard-managed clusters Identity provider OIDC login, user identity and role claims; bundled Keycloak or an existing provider Oracle Cloud / OKE The actual cloud resources and managed Kubernetes service The portal and services are delivered as released container images with Helm deployment assets. Customers pull approved images into their own environment or use an agreed internal registry mirror.

title: Architecture
heading: Request flow
text: The user signs in through the configured identity provider. The portal displays the templates, cluster options and limits available to that user. The API validates the request, compatibility and applicable configuration. A Terraform job executes with the installation's OCI permissions and cluster state. The portal exposes the run output and resulting cluster status. Lifecycle events are recorded for operational visibility. Protected destroy requests and requests for higher resource limits use the admin review workflow. This is not a general approval gate on every cluster creation or lifecycle action.

title: Architecture
heading: State and ownership
text: PostgreSQL stores platform metadata. Terraform state is stored in OCI Object Storage. Both are part of your operating and recovery responsibilities; backing up only the portal does not preserve the full platform state. Resources created by Infrayard are managed by their cluster's Terraform state. Manual edits to those managed resources can be overwritten by a subsequent apply. Supplied existing network resources are referenced according to the BYON ownership rules .

title: Architecture
heading: Connectivity and external dependencies
text: The installation must reach the required OCI APIs, configured identity provider and OKE API endpoints. Initial image delivery also requires registry access, or an agreed mirror. Optional SMTP notifications use your configured email service. Running the control plane in your tenancy does not remove these dependencies or automatically provide a disconnected deployment. Review the required routes and any delivery constraints during onboarding.

title: Architecture
heading: Operating responsibility
text: Your team operates the customer installation, its database, secrets, storage, network and workloads. Oracle provides the contracted OCI and OKE services. Solvia Lab supplies the Infrayard release, documentation and support defined in your agreement. Deployment assistance and additional operational support can be scoped in Enterprise. Continue with security and access , networking and operations .

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Overview
text: Use this page to assess deployment fit before committing to an installation. Exact versions, image references and customer-specific values are confirmed against the release supplied during onboarding.

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Deployment options
text: Requirement Existing OKE cluster Single-node k3s on OCI VM Intended use Production customer installations Evaluation, development and demos Deployment Customer Helm chart and OKE values The same chart with k3s values Ingress ingress-nginx with an OCI Load Balancer, configured separately Traefik, supplied by k3s Storage OCI Block Volume storage class ( oci-bv ) Local-path storage Identity Bundled Keycloak or an existing OIDC provider Bundled Keycloak or an existing OIDC provider Scheduling Dedicated worker nodes Single-node scheduling settings in the supplied values An existing supported Kubernetes host can run the platform; this does not imply that every Kubernetes distribution or version has been validated. Confirm the intended distribution and release during onboarding.

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Before installation
text: An OCI tenancy, target region and selected anchor compartment. A service identity with permissions for the resource families Infrayard will manage. OCI Object Storage configuration for Terraform state. A Kubernetes host with appropriate ingress, persistent storage and capacity for the platform services. DNS and TLS arrangements for the portal and identity endpoints. Network reachability from the runner and authorised users to the OKE API endpoints they will use. An approved image delivery path and the release-specific Helm assets. An identity provider configuration and admin role mapping. The installation includes PostgreSQL and identity services when configured in the supplied chart. Budget for these services, their persistent storage, any load balancer and your OKE resources. The software subscription does not pay your Oracle Cloud bill.

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: OKE versions, shapes and images
text: Compatibility is region- and tenancy-specific. Administrators sync OCI shapes and Kubernetes versions, then enable the choices available to users. Newly synced Kubernetes versions are disabled until an administrator enables them. The deploy and template forms filter Kubernetes versions by the selected shape and available OKE node images. If compatibility validation is unavailable, deployment is blocked rather than allowing an unverified combination. See troubleshooting .

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Basic and Enhanced clusters
text: The platform can allow Basic, Enhanced or both OKE tiers. These are Oracle service tiers, separate from Infrayard subscription plans. Operation Basic Enhanced Add or remove nodes and pools Supported automatically Supported automatically Change per-node shape, OCPU, RAM or storage Requires rolling worker cycling Automated supported rollout Kubernetes upgrade Control-plane and target updates, followed by rolling worker refresh Automated supported control-plane and worker rollout OCI control-plane charges Follow Oracle's Basic pricing Follow Oracle's Enhanced pricing Check cluster lifecycle for operational steps and workload considerations.

title: Requirements and compatibility
heading: Product scope
text: Current scope is OKE infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management through Infrayard workflows. The product includes templates, limits, protected requests, cost estimates, identity integration, audit records and supported existing-network configurations. Application deployment, CI/CD, databases used by your applications and application availability remain within your existing delivery and operating processes. Using an existing OKE cluster to host Infrayard is different from importing that cluster into Infrayard's Terraform management. Do not assume arbitrary existing clusters can be adopted; agree the supported lifecycle scope during evaluation. One installation's compartment access follows its anchor and OCI IAM scope. Unrelated compartment subtrees need an appropriate root anchor or separate installations. Existing subnets require an existing VCN reference and prepared routing. Some restricted public endpoint combinations require Infrayard-managed networking. AI assistance, the access agent and non-OCI management are roadmap items unless explicitly delivered in your contracted release. Hosting in your tenancy does not itself certify compliance, provide application high availability or create an air-gapped environment. See networking for supported combinations and releases and roadmap for future work.

title: Security and access
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard runs in the customer environment. OCI credentials, Terraform state, platform metadata and operational records are managed within that environment; a Solvia-hosted SaaS control plane is not required.

title: Security and access
heading: Identity and roles
text: Authentication uses OpenID Connect with the Authorization Code flow and PKCE. The browser does not store a confidential OIDC client secret. Use bundled Keycloak or connect an existing OIDC-compatible provider, such as Microsoft Entra ID, Okta or Google Workspace. Users are created on first login from their identity claim. An admin role grants access to the administration panel. Template role requirements can restrict which approved configurations a user sees. Role claim mapping is configured for your identity provider during onboarding. Changing template visibility or resource limits is not a substitute for reviewing OCI permissions and Kubernetes access rights. Review each layer against your organisation's access policy.

title: Security and access
heading: OCI credentials
text: The runner needs an OCI service identity with permissions for the resources it manages. Scope that identity to your selected anchor compartment and required resource families. A tenancy-root anchor needs correspondingly broader permissions. The exact policy statements and secret provisioning are part of the customer deployment runbook. Keep API keys, signing keys, database passwords and registry tokens in your approved secret-management process. Do not send them through website forms or include them in support attachments.

title: Security and access
heading: Kubernetes access
text: Authorised users can download a kubeconfig from a running cluster's detail page. The documented default uses a per-user Kubernetes ServiceAccount token, allowing kubectl access without local OCI CLI configuration. An explicit OCI-exec fallback is available for users who use OCI CLI authentication. export KUBECONFIG=~/oke-my-cluster-kubeconfig.yaml kubectl get nodes Authentication does not establish a network route. The user's machine and runner must reach the OKE API endpoint. See networking and connectivity . During security review, confirm the Kubernetes permissions, token lifetime, revocation procedure and downloaded credential handling for your supplied release. Website documentation is not a guarantee of a particular token expiry or a replacement for that review. Administrators can download access files for other users' clusters from All Clusters → Details . Include this privilege in your role review.

title: Security and access
heading: SSH access
text: Terraform-generated worker-node SSH keys are available through the documented cluster detail workflow. Treat downloaded private keys as credentials and retain them in your approved secure store. Confirm retrieval and rotation behaviour for your release; do not assume a later download will be available.

title: Security and access
heading: Audit and approvals
text: Lifecycle operations record actor, action, cluster, outcome and duration. Protected destroy requests and limit-increase requests record submission and review decisions. Administrators retain a privileged force-destroy path for incident response. The Activity inbox also records lifecycle events, request outcomes and limit changes. Optional SMTP notifications can send event details to configured recipients. Account for those emails when reviewing information flows and retention.

title: Security and access
heading: Network and delivery boundary
text: The installation still needs access to OCI APIs, its identity endpoints, required OKE endpoints and the approved registry delivery path. Optional SMTP and customer-selected integrations have their own destinations. Mirroring container images alone does not establish disconnected operation. Private endpoints and restricted public endpoints have different routing prerequisites. A future access agent is listed separately on the roadmap .

title: Security and access
heading: Customer security review
text: Review TLS, ingress exposure, IAM scope, Kubernetes roles, secrets, database access, state storage, backups, log access and operational access before production. Security questionnaires and additional evidence requirements can be scoped through Enterprise .

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Overview
text: Choose the endpoint model and ownership boundary before deployment. Kubernetes access files provide authentication; your runner and users still need a working network path.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Default setup
text: By default, Infrayard creates a full network stack per cluster: A VCN with a /16 range derived from the cluster's /24 CIDR A private worker subnet (/24) A public Kubernetes API endpoint subnet when public restricted API access is enabled A public load balancer subnet for Kubernetes LoadBalancer services Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, Service Gateway, and route tables for public/private paths Security lists with OKE-required ingress/egress rules plus API endpoint TCP/6443 allowlist rules

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Kubernetes API endpoint access
text: Admin Configuration includes Kubernetes API Access : Private endpoint keeps the OKE API on a private subnet. Infrayard and kubectl clients need an existing private route, VPN, or bastion path. Public endpoint restricted by CIDR allowlist creates a dedicated public API endpoint subnet and allows TCP/6443 only from configured CIDRs. Add both the Infrayard runner egress IP/range and company VPN/corporate egress ranges. 0.0.0.0/0 is rejected. This is the supported path when DRG is too costly and LPG does not scale past the per-VCN peering limit. Users still need to be on the corporate/VPN network for kubectl .

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Bringing your own network
text: Users can supply existing OCIDs via the Advanced tab in the deploy form. Infrayard skips creating whichever resources are already provided: Override Effect Existing VCN OCID Uses your VCN — skips VCN, IGW, gateway, and route table creation; generated subnets use the VCN's existing/default routing Existing Compartment OCID Places resources in your compartment — skips compartment creation Existing Subnet OCID Places nodes in your subnet — requires Existing VCN OCID, and skips subnet and security list creation Supported private-endpoint combinations: Combination Behavior No overrides Infrayard creates and manages the compartment, VCN, subnets, gateways, route tables, and security lists Existing Compartment OCID only Infrayard creates a new managed VCN/network stack inside that compartment Existing VCN OCID, with or without Existing Compartment OCID Infrayard reuses the VCN and creates cluster subnets/security lists inside it; existing VCN gateways and route tables are not managed Existing VCN OCID + Existing Subnet OCID, with or without Existing Compartment OCID True BYON networking: Infrayard creates OKE/node-pool resources and references the supplied network read-only Existing Subnet OCID without Existing VCN OCID Unsupported and rejected before Terraform starts Compartment subtree rule. Existing Compartment OCID must be a descendant (any depth) of the anchor compartment chosen at install time — the compartment Infrayard uses as the parent for new cluster compartments. The anchor is whatever existing compartment you point us at; it does not have to be a dedicated Infrayard-owned compartment. Direct children, grandchildren, and the anchor itself are all accepted. Siblings, ancestors, or compartments in unrelated subtrees are rejected with a 400 before Terraform starts — without this guard the deploy would fail mid- terraform apply with a confusing IAM error, because the runner's manage policies are scoped to the anchor subtree. Non-existent OCIDs return "compartment not found"; if OCI is briefly unreachable for the validation call, the API returns 503 so the deploy can simply be retried. The anchor is a knob, not a fixture. Pick the layout that matches your tenancy posture: Tenancy root anchor. No new compartments, nothing to rearrange — the entire tenancy is BYON-eligible. Right for "we don't want Infrayard adding any hierarchy on top of what we already have." Trade-off: the runner's IAM group needs manage permissions at tenancy scope (or scoped to the relevant resource families). Anchor at an existing org compartment. Slot Infrayard into a platforms , production , or infra compartment you already maintain. BYON works for anything under it, including peer compartments that already existed there. You don't have to create a new compartment to enable Infrayard. Dedicated anchor compartment. Create one (e.g. infrayard ) for explicit blast-radius isolation. Functionally identical to the previous case, just a narrower IAM scope. The single-install pattern that's not supported today is "one Infrayard spanning multiple unrelated subtrees of the same tenancy." That posture requires either tenancy-wide grants (use the tenancy-root anchor) or two installs. Restricted public API endpoint mode requires Infrayard-managed networking when Existing VCN OCID or Existing Subnet OCID would otherwise make the network read-only. Important behavior: Existing Compartment OCID does not auto-discover an existing VCN or subnet from that compartment. If VCN/subnet fields are left empty, Infrayard creates a new VCN/subnets/network stack inside the provided compartment. Advanced override UX guardrails: OCID fields validate type prefixes ( ocid1.vcn. , ocid1.compartment. , ocid1.subnet. ) and provide OCI-backed autocomplete lists for compartments, VCNs, and subnets. Shared compartment guidance: if you want multiple clusters in one compartment, use a dedicated BYO compartment via Existing Compartment OCID for all those clusters. Do not reuse a compartment that was auto-created for another cluster as a shared target. Note: If you deploy with existing VCN/subnet overrides, Infrayard does not manage route tables for those existing resources. Your existing network must already provide equivalent private-subnet egress required for OKE worker node registration: route 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT Gateway (or equivalent corporate egress path) and route all-<region>-services-in-oracle-services-network to a Service Gateway. This is a routing requirement, not an "open ingress" security rule. ⚠️ Drift behaviour. Infrayard-created VCN, subnet, IGW, route table, and security list resources are fully managed by the cluster's Terraform state — manual edits in the OCI Console will be overwritten on the next apply. Supplied BYO resources (existing VCN / subnet / compartment) are referenced read-only and never modified.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Custom security rules
text: Infrayard's default security list covers the ports required by OKE. For custom ingress/egress rules — exposing specific node ports, restricting egress to corporate CIDRs, or integrating with existing NSGs — the recommended approach is to bring your own subnet via the Advanced tab with your security configuration already applied. Infrayard uses your subnet and skips creating its own security list entirely, giving your network team full control without adding UI complexity.

title: Networking and existing infrastructure
heading: Pre-deployment review
text: Confirm the chosen endpoint mode, runner and client routes, anchor compartment, OCI policies, DNS and required service egress. Test reachability from the actual runner and authorised client network. Do not treat a VPN label or an existing subnet as proof that all routes are ready. See installation and security and access .

title: Installation
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard is deployed with the customer Helm chart into your environment. Registry access, pinned image references, customer values and the release-specific runbook are provided during evaluation or onboarding.

title: Installation
heading: Choose your deployment path
text: Existing OKE cluster: the production deployment path for teams with an appropriate Kubernetes host, ingress and persistent storage. Single-node k3s on an OCI VM: an evaluation and demo path using the same chart with values adapted for Traefik, local storage and single-node scheduling. It is not a substitute for a production availability design. See the requirements comparison . An OCI Marketplace deployment path is planned, rather than an installation option available from this website.

title: Installation
heading: Prepare your environment
text: Select the tenancy, region, anchor compartment and intended resource ownership boundary. Establish the OCI service identity and release-specific IAM policies. Prepare the OCI Object Storage state backend. Confirm host capacity, ingress, persistent storage, DNS and TLS. Agree an OIDC provider and configure the required endpoints and role claims. Check runner access to OCI services and OKE API endpoints, plus the intended user access path. Receive registry credentials and the pinned release, or arrange an approved mirror. Do not copy broad tenancy permissions from an unrelated deployment. Use the scope appropriate to your anchor compartment and network design .

title: Installation
heading: Install the supplied release
text: Create the image-pull secret and customer values described in the supplied runbook. Keep credentials out of shell history and source control. The following illustrates the Helm invocation once the chart and customer values are present: helm upgrade --install infrayard ./deploy/helm/ \ --namespace infrayard \ --create-namespace \ --values ./values.customer.yaml The chart path and values file above refer to delivered customer assets. They are not files available from the public website repository. Use the release-specific layout and approved image references supplied to you. OKE values use the configured ingress controller and OCI storage class. Evaluation k3s values use its ingress and local storage model. Review persistence and scheduling before applying a values file from another target.

title: Installation
heading: Verify the installation
text: Check that the deployed services and persistent volumes are healthy. Verify portal and identity URLs, TLS and successful login. Confirm the admin role and regular-user template visibility. Validate OCI access, the state backend, enabled shapes and Kubernetes versions. Create an appropriately scoped non-production cluster. Inspect Terraform logs, cluster state, the cost estimate and access download. Validate user connectivity and a suitable lifecycle operation. Clean up the test resources and review audit history. A successful Helm install alone does not validate your OCI policies, OKE worker network or end-user access path. Complete the workflow checks before production use.

title: Installation
heading: Evaluation readiness
text: Agree prerequisites and success criteria before starting an optional paid evaluation. Its 30-day window starts once the agreed environment is ready and the evaluation is activated. See evaluation terms . For errors, use troubleshooting and support . For repeatable operating procedures, continue with operations .

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Overview
text: These workflows apply to supported OKE clusters managed through Infrayard. Check your cluster tier and network prerequisites before making changes.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Signing in
text: Infrayard uses your organisation's existing identity provider (Keycloak, Azure AD, Okta, Google Workspace, or any OIDC-compliant IdP). Click Log In — you are redirected to your IdP's login page and returned to the portal after authentication. No separate Infrayard account is needed.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Deploying a cluster
text: Navigate to Deploy from the top nav (Optional) Select a Cluster template — pre-configured profiles created by your admin that pre-fill and lock resource fields (pools, nodes, CPU, RAM, storage). Choose "Custom" to configure everything manually with your account's limits enforced Enter a Cluster name — this becomes the base name for all OCI resources ( {name}-cluster , {name}-vcn , etc.) Choose a CIDR range from the available pool — each cluster gets its own /24 Select a Kubernetes version , VM shape , and Node image (locked if the template defines them; otherwise user-selectable — image defaults to auto-select if none configured) If using "Custom" mode, configure one or more Node pools — each pool has a name, node count, OCPU, RAM, and storage, constrained by your account's effective limits (Optional) Use the Advanced tab to bring existing OCI infrastructure — your own VCN, compartment, or subnet Review the Deployment Summary — shows all resources that will be created, plus live estimated monthly and hourly cost Click Deploy Infrayard runs terraform apply and streams the live output in the portal. The cluster appears in My Clusters once provisioning completes. The deploy form enforces your account's effective limits — maximum pools, nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage. If a limit prevents you from deploying, submit a limit-increase request from the deploy or scale flow; admins can approve granted values into your per-user overrides.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Scaling a cluster
text: In My Clusters , click Scale on a running cluster Adjust resources per pool — nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage Add new node pools or remove existing ones as needed; new pools default their name to the cluster's bare name and accept any name that matches the standard pool-name rules (lowercase, alphanumeric + hyphen, 32 chars max). Existing pool names stay immutable to keep Terraform/OKE state aligned. Review the change preview and click Apply Scaling behaviour depends on the cluster tier configured by your admin — see Cluster tiers . Kubernetes version changes are handled via a separate Upgrade action.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Destroying a cluster
text: In My Clusters , click Destroy Infrayard runs terraform plan -destroy and shows the exact resources that will be removed Confirm — terraform destroy runs and cluster-scoped OCI resources are cleaned up The CIDR range is returned to the pool and available for reuse Destroy is permanent and cannot be undone. Requests workflow: The admin Requests area handles both protected-cluster destroy approvals and per-user limit-increase requests. Users submit a reason instead of destroying directly or when they need higher limits; admins approve, adjust, or deny with a note. Destroy approval still opens the Terraform destroy plan before force-destroy. Limit approval writes granted values into the user's per-user overrides. Results appear in the user's Activity inbox, and SMTP-enabled installs can also send info-only email pings with requester, action, comments, and request parameters. Destroy behavior note: Infrayard-managed child compartments may be deleted with the cluster. External compartment overrides are retained for shared/multi-cluster setups. In Object Storage, only the destroyed cluster's .tfstate object is removed; the user-level prefix/folder is kept for other clusters.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Activity
text: The user nav includes an Activity inbox with an unread badge. It persists important events across refreshes and sessions; today it records destroy-request approvals/denials, limit request submissions and reviews, TTL expiry warnings at 24h, 4h, and 1h remaining, deploy/scale/upgrade/destroy start and completion events, and admin-driven account limit changes.

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Cluster detail
text: Click Details on any cluster card to see: Cluster information — name, status, K8s version, region, CIDR, compartment, VM shape, cluster tier, estimated monthly cost, OCID Node pools — pool name, node count, OCPU, RAM, storage, and status per pool Cost breakdown — per-pool monthly cost, control plane cost (Enhanced tier), and total with hourly rate Access — kubeconfig download and SSH key download (see Kubernetes access )

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Cluster tiers
text: The admin configures which cluster tier(s) the platform allows: Basic only , Enhanced only , or Both . When a single tier is allowed, users see it as an informational indicator on the deploy form. When Both is allowed, the deploy form shows a tier picker so each user picks per cluster — useful when one team wants free/dev clusters and another wants production-grade scaling, all served by the same platform. Basic Enhanced Cost Free Oracle's current Enhanced control-plane rate Node scaling ⚠️ Full — add/remove nodes or pools is automatic; resource-profile changes require manual cycling ✅ Full in-place Cluster Autoscaler ❌ ✅ Best for Dev/test, cost-sensitive teams Production, automated scaling Basic cluster scaling: Both Basic and Enhanced clusters support full scaling — nodes, OCPU, RAM, and storage. In Basic clusters, adding/removing nodes or node pools is automatic and does not require manual rotation. Manual cycling is required when changing per-node resources (shape, OCPU, RAM, storage), and is also recommended after a Kubernetes upgrade so workers pick up the new target image/version. OKE → Cluster → Node Pool → Nodes → Cordon & drain → Terminate Recommended rolling cycle for each affected Basic node pool (current size = N ): Scale from N to 2N Wait until the additional N nodes are Ready/Active Scale back from 2N to N (OKE removes extra nodes automatically) Verify workloads and node health before moving to the next pool The portal shows tier-specific warnings/messages for this flow. Kubernetes version upgrades: Use Upgrade k8s on a running cluster. This updates the control plane and node-pool target Kubernetes/image configuration: Direct upgrades are limited to the same or next minor version (for example 1.33.x -> 1.34.x ; not 1.33.x -> 1.35.x ). Basic: perform rolling worker refresh per pool ( N -> 2N -> N ) after nodes become Ready/Active ; the Upgrade modal shows live per-pool steps based on current node counts. Enhanced: rollout is fully automated (control plane plus worker refresh), no manual cycling required. Switching tiers: Admins can switch the platform tier at any time in Configuration — Basic, Enhanced, or Both. The change applies to all new clusters; existing clusters retain the tier they were provisioned with. Per-user tier override: Admins can pin a specific user to Basic or to Enhanced, regardless of the global setting. The override is force-only (single tier per user); a user without an override inherits whatever the global setting allows, including the per-cluster picker when the global is Both .

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Kubernetes upgrades
text: Dedicated action — available from cluster detail and dashboard actions Shape-aware + allowlist-aware — upgrade options are filtered to OCI-compatible versions enabled by admin config Sequential minors only — direct upgrades allow same/next minor only; skip-minor upgrades are blocked with explicit error Control plane + node-pool target update — upgrade action updates cluster Kubernetes and node-pool target version/image Basic upgrade behavior — perform rolling worker refresh per pool ( N -> 2N -> N ) after new nodes are Ready/Active Enhanced upgrade behavior — fully automated rollout (control plane + workers), no manual cycling required Tier guidance in UI — Basic and Enhanced show upgrade-specific notes with rollout guidance Dynamic Basic rollout guidance — Basic upgrade modal reads live pool/node counts and renders exact per-pool steps (for example 1 -> 2 -> 1 or 3 -> 6 -> 3 ) instead of a static example

title: Cluster lifecycle
heading: Expiry and cleanup
text: A time-to-live can be set for temporary clusters. When its TTL is reached, Infrayard starts the destroy workflow. Use TTL deliberately and review its interaction with your protected-cluster policy for the supplied release. Activity includes expiry warnings at 24 hours, 4 hours and 1 hour remaining. Scaling a Basic cluster to zero worker nodes can pause compute use, but does not guarantee a zero Oracle bill: retained resources and other services can still be charged. Review operating responsibilities before production changes.

title: Administration
heading: Overview
text: Administrators configure the approved options and operating boundaries available to each team. Review security and access for the identity and privilege model. Admin access is granted via your identity provider through role assignment — see customer integration docs (gated). Admins have a separate panel accessible from the top nav.

title: Administration
heading: All clusters
text: A full view of every cluster across all users — status, owner, CIDR, K8s version, tier, resource counts, estimated cost (monthly + hourly), and age. The stats cards show online, provisioning, upgrading k8s, destroying, failed, total, CIDRs used, and monthly spend. From this view admins can: Click Details on any cluster to open its full detail view including kubeconfig and SSH key download Click Scale on Active/Error clusters to adjust pools, nodes, and per-node resources Click Upgrade k8s on Active/Error clusters to upgrade Kubernetes version Click Destroy to destroy any cluster regardless of owner Click View logs while an operation is running or after a failure Click New Cluster to provision a cluster outside of normal user quotas

title: Administration
heading: Users & limits
text: Lists every user who has signed into Infrayard. For each user, admins can: View current cluster count and active limit View resolved effective limits (per-user override if set, otherwise global default) Click Edit Limits to set per-user overrides for any combination of: cluster limit, pool max, node max, OCPU, RAM, storage, and cluster tier Reset a user's overrides back to global defaults; direct admin limit edits and resets create user Activity notifications Reset all overrides at once to revert the user to global platform defaults Limit changes take effect on the user's next page load or login — no restart required.

title: Administration
heading: Configuration
text: Platform-wide settings manageable at runtime — no redeployment needed: Setting Description Cluster tier Basic (free), Enhanced (Oracle's current Enhanced control-plane rate), or Both — applies to all new clusters; "Both" lets the user pick per cluster on the deploy form Cluster limit Default max active clusters per user Node pool limit Max pools per cluster Nodes per pool Max nodes per pool OCPU / RAM / Storage Max compute per node CIDR pool Add, remove, and enable/disable /24 ranges available for cluster allocation VM shapes Sync from OCI, plus add/remove/enable/disable shapes in the deploy form K8s versions Add, remove, and enable/disable Kubernetes versions Node images Add, remove, and enable/disable OCI compute images for worker node pools Note: Shape and image availability is region- and tenancy-specific. In Admin → Configuration , use Sync from OCI in the VM Shapes section first, then curate/label as needed. For CLI verification, fetch current OKE node pool options in the target region: oci ce node-pool-options get --node-pool-option-id all --profile <PROFILE> Use the returned shapes and sources lists as the source of truth for VM shapes and node images. If Sync from OCI is unavailable, Infrayard keeps existing shape config unchanged and you can continue with manual curation from the CLI output above. Sync uses the API pod OCI service account credentials/policies (not the browser/user profile). K8s version freshness: OCI can publish new OKE patch versions after Infrayard is deployed. The platform now auto-syncs available OKE versions in the background (default daily) so admin config stays current without anyone clicking Refresh from OCI . Newly-fetched versions land disabled by default — admins still curate which versions users may deploy. Refresh from OCI remains available for on-demand pulls (e.g. before template reviews or upgrade waves). Upgrade recommendation pills use the latest enabled version, so stale enablement can hide available upgrades. Once a cluster's K8s version falls behind the latest enabled, a separate sweeper (default hourly) emits one Activity entry plus one email to the cluster owner per (cluster, target version) pair, so the owner is told about new upgrade options even when not actively logged in. The notification is idempotent — it does not re-fire for the same target — and the marker auto-resets after the cluster is upgraded, ready to fire again on the next enabled-version bump. Deploy form behavior: Kubernetes versions are filtered by the currently selected VM shape and region. Users only see versions that are both OCI-compatible for that shape (based on OKE node image availability) and enabled in Admin Configuration. If compatibility lookup is unavailable, the K8s list is not shown (fail-closed) and deploy is blocked until validation succeeds. If a version is missing, either enable it in Admin Configuration or choose a shape that supports it.

title: Administration
heading: Cluster templates
text: Templates are administrator-approved configurations. Template-defined resource values can exceed a user's personal custom-deployment limits; the locked fields prevent the user from editing those pre-approved values. Review template scope and required roles accordingly. Dedicated admin page for creating and managing cluster templates — pre-configured profiles that appear as selectable cards on the deploy form. Templates encode: Setting Description K8s version Pre-selected Kubernetes version (optional — user selects if not set) VM shape Pre-selected node shape (optional) Node image Pre-selected OCI compute image (optional — auto-selects latest OKE image if not set) Node pools Pre-defined pool layout — name, node count, OCPU, RAM, storage per pool Tier default Suggested cluster tier — Basic or Enhanced (suggestion only, not enforced) TTL Optional time-to-live in hours — when reached, Infrayard automatically starts cluster destroy/cleanup Destroy protection When enabled, the "Destroy" button on the user's cluster opens a "Request destroy" modal instead. Requests land in Admin → Requests (with a live count badge in the nav) where an admin approves, reviews the destroy plan, then confirms force-destroy, or denies with a note Required role Keycloak realm role — only users with this role can see and use the template (leave empty for all users) Sort order Controls display position in the deploy form (lower numbers appear first) The templates table shows estimated monthly and hourly cost per template. The add/edit modal includes a live cost preview that updates as you change pools, shape, or tier. Template modal behavior: when a VM shape is selected, the K8s dropdown is filtered to versions OCI reports as compatible for that shape in the current region (node-image-backed compatibility). If compatibility lookup is unavailable, no fallback list is shown (fail-closed). Template save/update re-validates shape+K8s compatibility and blocks incompatible combinations. Environment-tier gating — use required_role to control which teams can deploy which cluster sizes. For example, create a DEV — Small template visible to everyone, a TEST — Medium template requiring a testing role, a UAT — Large template requiring a uat role, and a PROD — HA template requiring a production role. Users only see the templates they have access to on the deploy form. Create the roles in Keycloak under Realm roles and assign them to the relevant users. Templates can be created, edited, enabled/disabled, and permanently deleted. Disabled templates no longer appear in the deploy form but remain referenced by existing clusters. Permanently deleting a template removes it from the admin panel entirely.

title: Administration
heading: Requests
text: Approval queue for user-submitted destroy requests on protection-enabled clusters and limit-increase requests for per-user overrides. The admin nav shows live request count badges that refresh every 5 seconds (hidden when zero pending). Filter by Pending / Approved / Denied / All. Each pending row has a Review action. When SMTP is configured, request submit/review events also send info-only email pings: admins get submit notifications, and users get submit/approve/deny notifications. For destroy requests, the review modal lets the admin: Add an optional admin note Click Approve & review plan — the normal destroy plan opens. After the admin confirms the plan, the request is marked approved and force=true destroy starts. Audit-logged as destroy-request:approve . Click Deny — the note is surfaced on the user's cluster card as a red "Destroy denied" pill (with the note in the tooltip). Audit-logged as destroy-request:deny . For limit requests, the review modal lets the admin grant the requested values or adjust them before approval. Approved values are written into the user's per-user overrides and the user receives an Activity notification. Denials can include an admin note and are audit-logged as limit-request:deny . Request emails include the requester, request id, comment, requested values, and granted values where applicable. Approval is row-locked to prevent two admins double-approving. Bypass path: admins can still force-destroy any protected cluster directly via ?force=true from the All Clusters table — useful for incident response.

title: Administration
heading: Audit Log
text: Every provisioning, scaling, upgrade, and destroy operation is recorded with user identity, operation type, cluster name, outcome, and duration — including destroy-request:* and limit-request:* events from the Requests queue. The log is append-only and filterable by user, operation, and date range.

title: Administration
heading: Resource limits
text: Limits cascade: global config sets the baseline for all users, per-user overrides take precedence when set. Limit Global default Per-user override Clusters per user Inherited from config ✅ Node pools per cluster 3 ✅ Nodes per pool 3 ✅ OCPU per node 1 ✅ RAM per node 12 GB ✅ Storage per node 50 GB ✅ Cluster tier BASIC_CLUSTER ✅ The deploy form always reflects the user's current effective limits. If a user hits a limit, the form shows a clear message with a link to contact support. Limits can be raised at any time by an admin without restarting the platform.

title: Administration
heading: Cost estimates
text: Cost estimates are visible in deployment forms, cluster cards, cluster details, templates and administrator views. They use configured resource rates with optional overrides for custom contracts. The breakdown covers the modelled compute, worker storage and control-plane components; it is not a reconciliation of your Oracle invoice. Review the rates and included components against your contract. Networking, load balancers, other services and the platform host can add charges outside the cluster estimate. Administrators can review estimated spend across active clusters. Estimates do not enforce a guaranteed monetary budget and do not include the Infrayard subscription.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Overview
text: The customer operates the Infrayard installation and the cloud environment around it. This page defines the operating areas to cover. Use the deployment and upgrade runbook for your supplied release for exact commands, supported versions and migration steps.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Responsibilities
text: Area Operating responsibility Kubernetes host, ingress, TLS, storage and network Customer, with deployment assistance if agreed OCI IAM and API credentials Customer PostgreSQL and Terraform state backup Customer Workload deployment, application backup and availability Customer Infrayard release images, documentation and contracted support Solvia Lab Extra rollout or incident assistance As scoped in the support agreement

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Before a platform upgrade
text: Record the installed image versions or digests, Helm release and customer values. Review the target release notes, compatibility requirements and any database migration guidance supplied with the release. Back up PostgreSQL, required deployment configuration and secrets using your approved tools. Preserve access to the related Terraform state in OCI Object Storage. Avoid scheduling a platform upgrade while cluster lifecycle jobs are running. Test the target release in a non-production installation where possible. Agree a maintenance window, validation plan and release-specific recovery procedure. Use the pinned, released image references supplied for the upgrade. Customer operators consume images; they do not need the product source code or maintainer build pipelines.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Validate after an upgrade
text: Sign in as an administrator and a representative regular user. Check role and template visibility, global limits and per-user overrides. Confirm cluster inventory, Activity history and audit records are available. Verify state-backend and OCI connectivity. Validate a suitable non-production lifecycle workflow before allowing wider changes.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Backups and recovery
text: Back up the database, relevant Helm values, necessary secrets and Terraform state under your organisation's retention and access controls. These contain different parts of the platform and need a consistent recovery plan. Define backup frequency, recovery point and recovery time requirements before production. Test restoring into an isolated environment. Do not assume that reinstalling Helm, reverting an image or recovering a single database snapshot will safely undo an infrastructure operation or database migration. During recovery, reconcile the restored metadata and state with the resources actually present in OCI before starting new jobs. Do not run competing Terraform operations against the same state. This public guide does not claim a built-in backup service, one-click rollback, or a particular recovery SLA. Any assisted recovery and response commitment is defined in your support agreement.

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: OKE and workload operations
text: An Infrayard platform upgrade and an OKE Kubernetes upgrade are separate changes. Worker refresh, disruption budgets, capacity, temporary scaling cost and application availability must be considered when scheduling OKE changes. See cluster lifecycle .

title: Operations, upgrades and recovery
heading: Ending a subscription
text: Arrange the supported handover of required configuration, access and state before the commercial access period ends. Ending a software subscription does not stop Oracle Cloud billing for resources left running. Subscription entitlements and the offboarding procedure are governed by your agreement; see billing and licensing .

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Overview
text: Start with the failing operation's execution logs and the affected cluster's detail page. Preserve the error and operation time before retrying. Confirm the actual OCI resource state before attempting a second infrastructure operation.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Missing versions or shapes
text: In Admin → Configuration , sync shapes and Kubernetes versions from OCI for the configured region. Newly discovered Kubernetes versions must be enabled by an administrator. The selected VM shape needs a compatible OKE node image. Compatibility lookup fails closed: an unavailable lookup can block deployment even if a version is enabled. Check runner credentials, OCI policies and API connectivity. If shape sync is unavailable, existing shape configuration remains in place for manual review. An administrator with an appropriately configured OCI CLI can inspect the current options: oci ce node-pool-options get --node-pool-option-id all --profile <PROFILE> Use region-appropriate results; do not copy a stale shape or image allowlist from another tenancy.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Existing-network validation fails
text: An existing subnet requires an existing VCN reference. The selected compartment must be within the installation's anchor scope. Reusing a compartment alone does not discover its VCN or subnets. Existing network resources need prepared routing and permissions. Restricted public endpoint mode is not supported with every read-only BYON combination. Review the networking combinations and ownership rules before changing permissions or resources.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Workers do not become ready
text: Inspect the OCI and Terraform error output, tenancy quotas, regional capacity and shape/image compatibility. For BYON private worker subnets, confirm the required egress path to OCI services. Network resources supplied by the customer are not automatically repaired by Infrayard.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Kubeconfig downloads but kubectl cannot connect
text: The kubeconfig supplies authentication, not routing. Check VPN or private-network access, endpoint mode and the configured TCP/6443 allowlist. Both the runner and relevant client networks need reachability. A downloaded file does not bypass a private endpoint or firewall.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: A limit prevents a request
text: Check the global default, per-user override and selected template. Submit a limit-increase request where offered; administrators can grant or adjust the values in the Requests queue. Approved templates can define pre-approved resource values that exceed a user's custom-configuration limits.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Login or role visibility is incorrect
text: Check the configured OIDC issuer, redirect addresses and role claims for the supplied release. Confirm admin and template role mapping. A user without a required template role will not see that template. Changes to limits are reflected on the next relevant load; a role change can require a fresh identity session.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Images cannot be pulled
text: Verify the released image references, registry entitlement, imagePullSecrets and network access to the approved registry or mirror. Contact support if a supplied registry credential has expired. Do not publish registry tokens in logs or screenshots.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: A lifecycle operation fails
text: Inspect the run output and OCI state. Failed deployments can expose a cleanup action for partial resources. Confirm what exists and what the action will remove before using it. For Basic clusters, review the required worker refresh after per-node changes or Kubernetes upgrades. Avoid manual edits to Infrayard-managed resources as a routine repair: the next Terraform apply can overwrite them. Where incident intervention is necessary, coordinate state reconciliation before running further jobs.

title: Troubleshooting and support
heading: Contact support
text: Email support@infrayard.eu or open the support form . Include: The installed Infrayard release and deployment option. The affected operation, approximate timestamp and region. The observed result and a sanitised error excerpt. Relevant recent changes and steps already attempted. Remove private keys, access tokens, passwords, customer data and unnecessary identifiers before sharing diagnostics. Response targets, support hours and escalation arrangements are defined by your subscription agreement. For additional support requirements, discuss Enterprise .

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Overview
text: Infrayard is commercial software deployed into the customer environment. Business can be purchased monthly or annually. Subscriptions and registry access are arranged directly with Solvia Lab through a commercial order and onboarding.

text: Billing option Price Commitment and payment Monthly €3,000 per month One billing month, paid in advance Annual €30,000 per year Twelve months, paid upfront; equivalent to €2,500 per month Annual payment saves €6,000 compared with twelve monthly payments. Oracle Cloud usage is billed separately by Oracle. Any applicable taxes and the contracted deployment scope are specified in your quote or invoice.

title: Subscription, billing and licensing

text: Business includes the commercial production subscription for the agreed installation scope, released images and deployment assets, core OKE lifecycle workflows, templates, role-based access, resource limits, protected requests, cost estimates, execution logs and activity history. It includes an onboarding workshop and email support. Business support has a 48-hour response SLA during the business hours defined in the agreement. Response is not a guaranteed incident resolution time. Your order identifies the covered installation and tenancy scope, support calendar and authorised contacts; this website does not imply unlimited installations, tenancies or managed-service resale. The customer operates the installation, OCI resources and workloads unless additional assistance is agreed. See operations and responsibilities .

text: The first 5 qualifying customers receive 40% off Business for their first 12 months. Billing option Founding price First-year comparison Monthly €1,800 per month Twelve payments total €21,600 Annual €18,000 for twelve months, paid upfront Equivalent to €1,500 per month The founding period begins when the production subscription starts. title: Subscription, billing and licensing

text: Enterprise starts from €6,500 per month. The proposal defines billing cadence, commitment, covered scope, deployment assistance, response times, escalation arrangements and any procurement or delivery requirements. A price shown per month does not establish an Enterprise cancellation right or a particular SLA. Those conditions are agreed in the proposal. Discuss your requirements .

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Evaluation
text: A paid evaluation is optional. After a demo and prerequisite review, a customer can start a monthly production subscription directly. The optional guided evaluation costs €1,500 for 30 days in your own tenancy, for non-production validation. Agree scope, success criteria and environment readiness first. The window starts when the agreed prerequisites are ready and the evaluation is activated. The evaluation includes a guided deployment session, evaluation instructions, time-limited registry access and business-hours email support. Oracle usage remains payable to Oracle. Evaluation access ends with the agreed evaluation period; production use requires a production subscription. The full evaluation fee is credited once against your first production invoice if the production order is accepted within 30 days after the evaluation ends. This applies to monthly or annual Business, qualifying Founding Business or an agreed Enterprise order. The fee is not described as a refundable deposit. Discuss an evaluation .

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Change from monthly to annual
text: You can request an annual term after starting monthly. Agree the transition date and credit for any unused, already paid subscription time before the annual invoice is issued. The annual term then runs for twelve months from the agreed start date. A billing change does not restart the founding discount period; any founding-period transition is documented in the revised order.

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Cancellation and offboarding
text: Monthly Business can be cancelled before the next renewal by contacting hello@infrayard.eu . It ends at the close of the current paid billing period. Annual subscriptions cover the full paid twelve-month term. Refunds, Enterprise commitments and any exceptional termination rights follow the signed commercial terms. Agree offboarding before access ends, including required configuration, operational records, Terraform state and supported credential handover. Production licence rights, updates, registry access and support follow the entitlement period and the agreement. Do not assume that cancelling the software subscription deletes or stops OCI resources; Oracle usage charges continue for resources left running.

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Licence and delivery
text: The commercial agreement governs production rights, deployment scope and restrictions. Standard delivery includes released images, registry access, Helm deployment assets and documentation. Product source code and release automation are not included unless separately agreed. Managed-service resale and redistribution require explicit written permission. This public website and documentation do not grant an open-source or Business Source License to the commercial product and do not change rights granted under any separately issued licence. See the website legal notice and your commercial agreement.

title: Subscription, billing and licensing
heading: Start a subscription
text: Request a demo or contact hello@infrayard.eu . We confirm product fit, deployment scope and terms before arranging access. The public website does not collect a card payment or automatically provision a subscription.

title: Releases and roadmap
heading: Overview
text: Choose Infrayard based on capabilities available in the release delivered to your organisation. Planned work is described separately below and is not a delivery commitment unless included in a written agreement.

title: Releases and roadmap
heading: Available capabilities
text: Create, scale, upgrade, access and destroy OKE clusters through the portal. Inspect Terraform execution logs and lifecycle status. Publish cluster templates and control role visibility. Configure global limits, per-user overrides and limit-increase requests. Protect cluster destruction with an admin review workflow. Use supported existing OCI compartments, VCNs and subnets. Download Kubernetes access files without requiring local OCI CLI setup in the default access workflow. Review cost estimates, Activity notifications and audit history. Sync available shapes and Kubernetes versions with compatibility filtering. Use customer-managed identity and a Helm-based customer installation. Operational behaviour depends on cluster tier and network design; see requirements and cluster lifecycle .

title: Releases and roadmap
heading: Versioned delivery
text: Customers receive released container images, pinned references, deployment values and applicable release guidance. Images can be pulled from the approved delivery registry or an agreed mirror. Source code and maintainer CI are not required for customer deployment. Use the version and upgrade notes included with your supplied release. This public page does not assign invented release dates or release numbers to the current build. Track the exact image versions or digests running in your installation.
